items.title: I can define a group using all four required conditions
items.what: A group is two or more people who interact, influence each other, and share a common goal. All four conditions must be present: minimum two members, mutual interaction, mutual influence, and a shared objective.
items.why: Being precise about what constitutes a group prevents confusing it with a mere collection of people, which matters when analysing whether group dynamics apply to a given situation.
items.example: Two strangers waiting at a bus stop heading to the same destination do not form a group, because although they share a destination, they are not interacting or influencing each other.

subtopic.name: Social Groups and Culture
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the psychological definition of a group, how group membership shapes behaviour through norms, social loafing, and social identity, and how individualist and collectivist cultures produce different behavioural patterns.
subtopic.why: Understanding these forces helps explain why people act differently depending on who they are with and which culture they belong to, including behaviours that may seem surprising when viewed in isolation.

items.title: I can distinguish between in-groups and out-groups and explain why a person can have multiple of each
items.what: An in-group is any group an individual belongs to or identifies with; an out-group is any group they do not. Because people hold multiple social identities simultaneously, they can belong to several in-groups at once, each with its own corresponding out-groups.
items.why: Recognising the in-group/out-group distinction helps explain many everyday social tensions and biases, including why people favour their own team, school, or nationality over others.
items.example: A student might have their school as one in-group and their school's football team as a second in-group, making students from rival schools an out-group at one level and non-football-playing schoolmates a different out-group at another.

subtopic.name: Social Groups and Culture
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the psychological definition of a group, how group membership shapes behaviour through norms, social loafing, and social identity, and how individualist and collectivist cultures produce different behavioural patterns.
subtopic.why: Understanding these forces helps explain why people act differently depending on who they are with and which culture they belong to, including behaviours that may seem surprising when viewed in isolation.

items.title: I can distinguish between formal and informal group norms and give an example of each
items.what: Formal norms are explicitly stated rules, such as a contract clause requiring attendance at practice. Informal norms are unspoken expectations learned through social consequences, such as knowing to take turns paying for meals in a friendship group.
items.why: Both types of norms regulate behaviour and carry consequences for non-compliance, but informal norms are often harder to identify because they are never written down, making them easy to violate unintentionally.
items.example: A workplace requiring employees to arrive by 9 am is a formal norm. The expectation that colleagues greet each other in the morning is an informal norm, because no policy states it, yet ignoring it may lead to social friction.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the psychological definition of a group, how group membership shapes behaviour through norms, social loafing, and social identity, and how individualist and collectivist cultures produce different behavioural patterns.
subtopic.why: Understanding these forces helps explain why people act differently depending on who they are with and which culture they belong to, including behaviours that may seem surprising when viewed in isolation.

items.title: I can explain the social identity theory and link it to in-group favouritism and out-group discrimination
items.what: Social identity theory holds that people favour their in-group over out-groups to protect and enhance their own self-esteem. This tendency can escalate to prejudice and discrimination when out-groups are perceived as threatening the in-group's status.
items.why: The theory explains why even mild group membership, such as being assigned to a team in a classroom activity, can generate favouritism and hostility toward others, with serious real-world consequences including racism and sectarianism.
items.example: A football supporter who considers themselves generally kind may find themselves insulting players from the opposing team during a match, behaviour driven by social identity theory rather than personal malice.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the psychological definition of a group, how group membership shapes behaviour through norms, social loafing, and social identity, and how individualist and collectivist cultures produce different behavioural patterns.
subtopic.why: Understanding these forces helps explain why people act differently depending on who they are with and which culture they belong to, including behaviours that may seem surprising when viewed in isolation.

items.title: I can define social loafing and identify conditions that promote or prevent it
items.what: Social loafing is the reduction in individual effort that occurs when working in a group, driven by the belief that others will compensate. It is more likely on easy or personally unimportant tasks, and is reduced when individual contributions are identifiable or group interaction is high.
items.why: Awareness of social loafing is practically useful for designing group tasks, assigning accountability, and understanding why people who are motivated individually sometimes underperform in teams.
items.example: In a group science project where all members share a single grade, a student who dislikes science may contribute minimally. Adding a requirement that each student writes their name beside the section they completed tends to reduce this loafing.

subtopic.name: Social Groups and Culture
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the psychological definition of a group, how group membership shapes behaviour through norms, social loafing, and social identity, and how individualist and collectivist cultures produce different behavioural patterns.
subtopic.why: Understanding these forces helps explain why people act differently depending on who they are with and which culture they belong to, including behaviours that may seem surprising when viewed in isolation.

items.title: I can compare individualist and collectivist cultures across work, family, and social domains
items.what: Individualist cultures, common in Western societies like Australia, prioritise personal goals, independence, and individual achievement. Collectivist cultures, common in many East Asian societies, prioritise group harmony, interdependence, and shared responsibility.
items.why: Cultural orientation shapes everyday decisions around career, family care, and social interaction. Recognising these differences helps avoid misinterpreting culturally typical behaviour as unusual or rude.
items.example: When offered a better-paying job at a rival company, a person from an individualist culture is more likely to accept it for personal gain, whereas a person from a collectivist culture is more likely to negotiate improved terms with their current employer to avoid disrupting the team.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the psychological definition of a group, how group membership shapes behaviour through norms, social loafing, and social identity, and how individualist and collectivist cultures produce different behavioural patterns.
subtopic.why: Understanding these forces helps explain why people act differently depending on who they are with and which culture they belong to, including behaviours that may seem surprising when viewed in isolation.

items.title: I can explain how cultural norms become internalised over time
items.what: When a person is raised within a consistent culture, its norms are gradually absorbed and come to feel like personal values rather than external rules. This means people often follow cultural norms not out of fear of punishment but because those norms genuinely align with their sense of self.
items.why: This internalisation explains why cross-cultural misunderstandings arise: a behaviour that feels obviously correct to one person may seem rude or strange to someone from a different cultural background, because each is drawing on deeply held, internalised norms.
items.example: Marlin, raised in an individualist culture, behaves assertively and competitively at work without realising it, because this was always normal. When he moves to China, his collectivist colleagues find the same behaviour inappropriate, creating conflict despite Marlin having no intention to offend.

subtopic.why: Understanding these forces helps explain why people act differently depending on who they are with and which culture they belong to, including behaviours that may seem surprising when viewed in isolation.

items.title: I can define obedience and identify three factors that increase its likelihood
items.what: Obedience is complying with commands from a perceived authority figure. The three main factors increasing obedience are: higher status or power of the authority figure, greater physical or relational proximity to that figure, and observing others obeying the same commands.
items.why: Knowing these factors helps explain why authority symbols such as uniforms, proximity, and social proof are so effective at producing compliance, and why people in positions of authority carry significant responsibility.
items.example: A student is more likely to sit down when instructed by a teacher standing right next to them (high proximity and high status) than when a classmate calls out the same instruction from across the room (low status, low proximity).

subtopic.name: Obedience and Conformity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the psychological concepts of obedience and conformity, the factors that influence each, the landmark experiments by Milgram (1963) and Asch (1951), contemporary replications, and the ethical issues these studies raise.
subtopic.why: Both obedience and conformity are present in everyday life and can lead people to act in ways they would not choose individually, ranging from following reasonable authority to participating in harm. Understanding the mechanisms behind them supports more critical thinking about one's own behaviour.

items.title: I can describe the aim, procedure, and results of Milgram's (1963) obedience experiment
items.what: Milgram aimed to test how far 40 male participants would obey an experimenter's instructions to administer electric shocks of increasing voltage to a confederate acting as a learner. Despite visible distress in many participants, 65% (26 of 40) continued to the maximum 450 volts.
items.why: The results were far higher than any expert predicted beforehand, demonstrating that ordinary people can cause serious harm to others when instructed by a perceived authority, a finding with direct relevance to understanding atrocities like the Holocaust.
items.example: Before the study, 14 Yale psychology students predicted on average that only about 1.2% of participants would administer the maximum shock. The actual result was 65%, showing how dramatically humans underestimate the power of authority.

subtopic.name: Obedience and Conformity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the psychological concepts of obedience and conformity, the factors that influence each, the landmark experiments by Milgram (1963) and Asch (1951), contemporary replications, and the ethical issues these studies raise.
subtopic.why: Both obedience and conformity are present in everyday life and can lead people to act in ways they would not choose individually, ranging from following reasonable authority to participating in harm. Understanding the mechanisms behind them supports more critical thinking about one's own behaviour.

items.title: I can evaluate Milgram's experiment against at least two ethical guidelines
items.what: Milgram's experiment breached three key ethical standards: the no-harm principle (participants experienced psychological distress and a 45-volt real shock), withdrawal rights (participants were told to continue despite wanting to leave), and informed consent/debriefing (participants were deceived about the study's true purpose).
items.why: Evaluating studies against ethical guidelines is a required skill in VCE Psychology and reflects the broader principle that scientific value does not justify causing lasting harm to participants.
items.example: When participants verbally said they wanted to stop, the experimenter responded with scripted phrases such as 'the experiment requires you continue,' which pressured them to stay despite their right to withdraw without penalty.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the psychological concepts of obedience and conformity, the factors that influence each, the landmark experiments by Milgram (1963) and Asch (1951), contemporary replications, and the ethical issues these studies raise.

Understanding the mechanisms behind them supports more critical thinking about one's own behaviour.

items.title: I can describe the key findings of Caspar et al. (2016) and explain what they add to our understanding of obedience
items.what: Caspar et al. found that when participants were ordered to press a key that delivered a mild shock, they perceived their action as more passive than when they chose freely, suggesting that being ordered to act reduces a person's felt sense of responsibility and agency.
items.why: This study updates Milgram's findings using ethical methods with genuine informed consent. It suggests that obedience works partly by allowing people to psychologically distance themselves from the consequences of their actions.
items.example: In the study, participants judged the time between pressing a key and hearing a tone as longer when ordered than when choosing freely, indicating their actions felt less like their own when commanded, even when no harm was caused.

subtopic.name: Obedience and Conformity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the psychological concepts of obedience and conformity, the factors that influence each, the landmark experiments by Milgram (1963) and Asch (1951), contemporary replications, and the ethical issues these studies raise.
subtopic.why: Both obedience and conformity are present in everyday life and can lead people to act in ways they would not choose individually, ranging from following reasonable authority to participating in harm. Understanding the mechanisms behind them supports more critical thinking about one's own behaviour.

items.title: I can define conformity and identify four factors that influence it
items.what: Conformity is adjusting thoughts, feelings, or behaviours to match those of others, a social group, or a social situation. Four factors that increase conformity are: social norms, groupthink, group shift, and deindividuation.
items.why: Conformity is often invisible in everyday life because it feels natural, yet it can lead individuals to behave in ways they later regret or find inconsistent with their values, as seen in bystander inaction and online bullying.
items.example: At a crowded public pool where nobody else is responding to a person in distress, an individual may conform to the group's inaction due to deindividuation, feeling neither visible nor personally responsible for helping.

subtopic.name: Obedience and Conformity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the psychological concepts of obedience and conformity, the factors that influence each, the landmark experiments by Milgram (1963) and Asch (1951), contemporary replications, and the ethical issues these studies raise.
subtopic.why: Both obedience and conformity are present in everyday life and can lead people to act in ways they would not choose individually, ranging from following reasonable authority to participating in harm. Understanding the mechanisms behind them supports more critical thinking about one's own behaviour.

items.title: I can describe the aim, procedure, and results of Asch's (1951) conformity experiment
items.what: Asch had 50 male university students complete a line-matching task in groups where all other members were confederates instructed to give a unanimously incorrect answer on 12 of 18 trials. Of the real participants, 74% conformed to at least one wrong answer, while 24% never conformed.
items.why: Asch's results show that social pressure is powerful enough to make people doubt clear perceptual evidence, demonstrating that conformity is driven more by the discomfort of standing out than by any genuine uncertainty about the correct answer.
items.example: Even participants who never conformed reported feeling confused and doubting their own correct answers during the study, showing that the pressure to conform was felt by everyone, not just those who gave in to it.

subtopic.name: Obedience and Conformity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the psychological concepts of obedience and conformity, the factors that influence each, the landmark experiments by Milgram (1963) and Asch (1951), contemporary replications, and the ethical issues these studies raise.
subtopic.why: Both obedience and conformity are present in everyday life and can lead people to act in ways they would not choose individually, ranging from following reasonable authority to participating in harm. Understanding the mechanisms behind them supports more critical thinking about one's own behaviour.

items.title: I can compare obedience and conformity using their key similarities and differences
items.what: Both obedience and conformity influence individual behaviour and occur in everyday life. The key difference is that obedience involves a direct command from an authority figure with punishment as the consequence of refusal, whereas conformity involves indirect social pressure from a group with social rejection as the consequence of non-compliance.
items.why: Distinguishing the two concepts is necessary for correctly identifying which mechanism is operating in a given scenario, an exam skill that requires careful attention to whether a direct command or indirect group pressure is driving the behaviour.
items.example: A student who sits down because a teacher tells them to is demonstrating obedience. The same student sitting down because everyone else in the class already has, without being told to, is demonstrating conformity.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the psychological concepts of obedience and conformity, the factors that influence each, the landmark experiments by Milgram (1963) and Asch (1951), contemporary replications, and the ethical issues these studies raise.
subtopic.why: Both obedience and conformity are present in everyday life and can lead people to act in ways they would not choose individually, ranging from following reasonable authority to participating in harm. Understanding the mechanisms behind them supports more critical thinking about one's own behaviour.

items.title: I can describe Sun and Yu's (2016) conformity study and explain what it shows about the age at which conformity emerges
items.what: Sun and Yu showed kindergarten children a photo of a face, had them rate its attractiveness, then showed them fake peer ratings before asking them to rate again. Children around age six tended to shift their ratings toward the group's rating, while younger children did not.
items.why: This finding extends the relevance of Asch's research to young children and suggests that conformity to peer influence develops around age six, which has implications for education and understanding social development.
items.example: A five-year-old who rated a face as 4 out of 8 was unlikely to change their rating after seeing peers rate it as 6, whereas a six-year-old in the same situation was likely to revise their rating upward to match the group.

items.title: I can distinguish between print and digital media and give examples of each
items.what: Print media refers to information displayed on a physical surface, such as newspapers and magazines. Digital media refers to information projected onto an electronic device, including social media platforms, television, and video games.
items.why: The distinction matters because digital media, particularly the internet and smartphones, has dramatically expanded the speed, reach, and interactivity of information, creating new behavioural influences that print media did not produce.
items.example: A billboard advertisement for a car brand is print media. The same advertisement appearing as a targeted post in a social media feed is digital media, and can be tailored, shared, and commented on in real time.

subtopic.name: Media and Behaviour
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how print and digital media influence individual and group behaviour through four mechanisms: changes to social connections, social comparison, addictive behaviours, and information access.
subtopic.why: Media is now inescapable in daily life, meaning its capacity to shape self-perception, social relationships, and access to information affects virtually everyone. Evaluating these influences as both positive and negative is a core critical thinking skill.

items.title: I can explain what technological determinism proposes about media and behaviour
items.what: Technological determinism is the theory that technology unavoidably determines cultural and social change, and that the medium itself, rather than any specific piece of content, is what drives changes in behaviour.
items.why: This framework helps explain why the arrival of television, and later smartphones, produced widespread shifts in daily routines and social interaction that no single program or app could account for on its own.
items.example: Families timing dinner around a nightly television program illustrates technological determinism: the behaviour change is caused by television as a medium, not by the specific content of any one show.

subtopic.name: Media and Behaviour
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how print and digital media influence individual and group behaviour through four mechanisms: changes to social connections, social comparison, addictive behaviours, and information access.
subtopic.why: Media is now inescapable in daily life, meaning its capacity to shape self-perception, social relationships, and access to information affects virtually everyone. Evaluating these influences as both positive and negative is a core critical thinking skill.

items.title: I can evaluate the positive and negative effects of media on social connections at both individual and group levels
items.what: Positive effects include expanded ability to maintain relationships across distances and access online support. Negative effects include social fatigue from pressure to stay constantly connected, the formation of shallow online relationships that produce feelings of isolation, and the risk of false or unsafe online identities.
items.why: Social connections are a fundamental contributor to mental wellbeing, so understanding how media shapes them, for better and worse, is central to analysing media's overall impact on human behaviour.
items.example: On the positive side, around 300,000 Australians joined the 2019 climate strike, a gathering largely organised via social media. On the negative side, large online group chats can pressure individuals to participate in cyberbullying to match the behaviour of others in the group.

subtopic.name: Media and Behaviour
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how print and digital media influence individual and group behaviour through four mechanisms: changes to social connections, social comparison, addictive behaviours, and information access.
subtopic.why: Media is now inescapable in daily life, meaning its capacity to shape self-perception, social relationships, and access to information affects virtually everyone. Evaluating these influences as both positive and negative is a core critical thinking skill.

items.title: I can define social comparison and explain how media can produce both high and low self-esteem
items.what: Social comparison is the tendency to measure one's own self-worth by comparing oneself to others. Media can trigger upward comparisons to idealised or curated profiles, producing lower self-esteem, or downward comparisons to others with less skill or experience, producing higher self-esteem.
items.why: Because social media platforms encourage users to present idealised versions of themselves, the comparisons they invite are often unrealistic, creating a measurable risk of body-image anxiety and low self-worth, particularly in susceptible groups.
items.example: An experienced hiker who sees beginners starting out on social media may feel confident about their own skill level. However, a person with low body confidence who regularly sees filtered model images in advertisements may experience increased body-image anxiety, as found by Dittmar and Howard in 2004.

subtopic.name: Media and Behaviour
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how print and digital media influence individual and group behaviour through four mechanisms: changes to social connections, social comparison, addictive behaviours, and information access.
subtopic.why: Media is now inescapable in daily life, meaning its capacity to shape self-perception, social relationships, and access to information affects virtually everyone. Evaluating these influences as both positive and negative is a core critical thinking skill.

items.title: I can define addictive behaviours in the context of media and explain the role of attentional bias
items.what: Addictive behaviours are behaviours associated with dependence on a particular stimulus despite negative consequences. In a media context, an addictive behaviour might involve continuing to play online games during class despite falling behind. Attentional bias occurs when addictive stimuli, or cues associated with them, distract attention away from other tasks.
items.why: While debate remains about whether media such as social media is inherently addictive, the concept of attentional bias helps identify when media use has crossed from habitual engagement into a pattern that impairs functioning.
items.example: A student who is addicted to a mobile game may find their attention pulled toward their phone every time a notification sound plays during class, even when they intend to focus on the lesson. This captures the nature of attentional bias in media addiction.

subtopic.name: Media and Behaviour
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how print and digital media influence individual and group behaviour through four mechanisms: changes to social connections, social comparison, addictive behaviours, and information access.
subtopic.why: Media is now inescapable in daily life, meaning its capacity to shape self-perception, social relationships, and access to information affects virtually everyone. Evaluating these influences as both positive and negative is a core critical thinking skill.

items.title: I can assess information access as both a positive and negative influence of media on behaviour
items.what: Information access refers to how easily information can be reached by different people. Digital media has made this faster and more widespread than ever before, enabling rapid responses to emergencies and personal research. However, the same infrastructure allows misinformation to spread without restriction.
items.why: The speed of digital information transmission can save lives in medical emergencies but can also cause significant harm when false information, such as unproven health claims during a pandemic, spreads before it can be corrected.
items.example: During the early COVID-19 pandemic, false claims that sipping water every 15 minutes would prevent infection spread widely on social media, giving some people false reassurance and potentially reducing uptake of evidence-based protective measures.

subtopic.what: This subtopic examines how print and digital media influence individual and group behaviour through four mechanisms: changes to social connections, social comparison, addictive behaviours, and information access.
subtopic.why: Media is now inescapable in daily life, meaning its capacity to shape self-perception, social relationships, and access to information affects virtually everyone. Evaluating these influences as both positive and negative is a core critical thinking skill.

items.title: I can define independence and explain how it differs from simply ignoring social norms
items.what: Independence means being free from the control or influence of others when making decisions, with choices driven by personal beliefs and intrinsic motivation rather than external pressure. An independent person may still choose behaviours that align with group norms, but the driver of that choice is internal.
items.why: Independence is often confused with deliberate rule-breaking, but a truly independent person acts authentically regardless of whether that action happens to match or contradict group expectations.
items.example: A student who dresses in a way considered unfashionable, simply because they prefer that style, is demonstrating independence. A student who deliberately wears something unfashionable to annoy others is displaying anti-conformity rather than independence.

subtopic.name: Empowering Individual Decision-Making
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how independence develops through the self-determination theory and its three psychological needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness), and how anti-conformity can be encouraged through reactance, individuation, the desire to promote change, and social support.
subtopic.why: Understanding the psychological conditions that allow individuals to act on their own values rather than group pressure is important for evaluating individual behaviour in real-world contexts and for recognising how people can resist harmful social influences.

items.title: I can distinguish between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation and link intrinsic motivation to self-determination
items.what: Extrinsic motivation involves engaging in behaviours for external rewards such as money, praise, or avoiding negative judgment. Intrinsic motivation involves engaging in behaviours for internal rewards such as personal growth, curiosity, or satisfaction. Self-determination, and therefore independence, is primarily driven by intrinsic motivation.
items.why: People who are primarily extrinsically motivated remain dependent on others to define what is worth doing, making them more susceptible to social pressure. Shifting toward intrinsic motivation is therefore central to developing independence.
items.example: A student who studies psychology because they find human behaviour genuinely fascinating is intrinsically motivated. A student who studies it only to please their parents is extrinsically motivated and may be more likely to change their choices if parental expectations shift.

subtopic.name: Empowering Individual Decision-Making
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how independence develops through the self-determination theory and its three psychological needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness), and how anti-conformity can be encouraged through reactance, individuation, the desire to promote change, and social support.
subtopic.why: Understanding the psychological conditions that allow individuals to act on their own values rather than group pressure is important for evaluating individual behaviour in real-world contexts and for recognising how people can resist harmful social influences.

items.title: I can name and define the three basic psychological needs in self-determination theory
items.what: The self-determination theory, developed by Ryan and Deci, identifies three needs that must all be met for full independence: autonomy (acting based on personal choice and intrinsic motivation), competence (having the skills to carry out meaningful actions), and relatedness (feeling a genuine sense of belonging and connection to others).
items.why: Because all three needs must be fulfilled for true independence to develop, identifying which need is unmet in a given scenario allows a precise explanation of why someone is not acting independently.
items.example: Cody feels connected to friends (relatedness met) and believes he can choose his own path (autonomy met), but doubts his academic abilities (competence not met). This unfulfilled need prevents him from fully acting on his own values without being swayed by others' opinions.

subtopic.name: Empowering Individual Decision-Making
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how independence develops through the self-determination theory and its three psychological needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness), and how anti-conformity can be encouraged through reactance, individuation, the desire to promote change, and social support.
subtopic.why: Understanding the psychological conditions that allow individuals to act on their own values rather than group pressure is important for evaluating individual behaviour in real-world contexts and for recognising how people can resist harmful social influences.

items.title: I can explain how each of the three self-determination needs specifically promotes independent decision-making in a group context
items.what: Autonomy supports independent decision-making by increasing belief that one's individual actions are meaningful. Competence reduces susceptibility to social influence by increasing confidence in one's own judgment. Relatedness supports independence when peers are supportive rather than controlling, removing the fear of social rejection.
items.why: These mechanisms explain how group settings can either suppress or support independence, and provide a framework for understanding why some people resist social pressure more effectively than others.
items.example: A skilled debater (competence met) who believes their vote counts (autonomy met) and whose family supports their choices (relatedness met) is more likely to vote according to their own research than to match the opinions of a social group.

subtopic.name: Empowering Individual Decision-Making
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how independence develops through the self-determination theory and its three psychological needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness), and how anti-conformity can be encouraged through reactance, individuation, the desire to promote change, and social support.
subtopic.why: Understanding the psychological conditions that allow individuals to act on their own values rather than group pressure is important for evaluating individual behaviour in real-world contexts and for recognising how people can resist harmful social influences.

items.title: I can define anti-conformity and explain why it must be deliberate to qualify as anti-conformity
items.what: Anti-conformity is a deliberate refusal to comply with social norms or standards, involving both active resistance to the expectations of others and the purposeful expression of attitudes or behaviours that challenge those norms. Non-conformity that is accidental, such as a tourist unknowingly breaking a local custom, does not qualify.
items.why: The deliberate nature of anti-conformity is what distinguishes it psychologically: research by Seery et al. found that intentional deviation from group opinion produces a physiological 'challenge' state, whereas unintentional deviation produces a 'threat' state.
items.example: A model who deliberately posts unfiltered photos on Instagram to challenge unrealistic beauty standards is engaging in anti-conformity. A person who simply never learned that filters were expected is not, because there is no deliberate refusal.

subtopic.name: Empowering Individual Decision-Making
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how independence develops through the self-determination theory and its three psychological needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness), and how anti-conformity can be encouraged through reactance, individuation, the desire to promote change, and social support.
subtopic.why: Understanding the psychological conditions that allow individuals to act on their own values rather than group pressure is important for evaluating individual behaviour in real-world contexts and for recognising how people can resist harmful social influences.

items.title: I can identify and explain four factors that encourage anti-conformity
items.what: Four factors encourage anti-conformity: the desire to promote change (a belief that current norms are unjust), reactance (motivational resistance triggered when personal freedom is threatened), individuation (being visible and identifiable within a group, increasing felt responsibility), and social support (having at least one other person who shares your position).
items.why: These factors either provide the motivation to act against norms or weaken the forces that make conformity feel necessary. Understanding them allows analysis of real-world cases where individuals resist group pressure.
items.example: A teenager who wants to attend a school climate strike during class hours is more likely to do so if one friend joins them (social support) and if a teacher uses language like 'you must stay in school' (reactance). Either factor alone increases the likelihood of anti-conformist action.

subtopic.name: Empowering Individual Decision-Making
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how independence develops through the self-determination theory and its three psychological needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness), and how anti-conformity can be encouraged through reactance, individuation, the desire to promote change, and social support.
subtopic.why: Understanding the psychological conditions that allow individuals to act on their own values rather than group pressure is important for evaluating individual behaviour in real-world contexts and for recognising how people can resist harmful social influences.

items.title: I can explain how anti-conformity and independence relate to each other and why an independent person does not always display anti-conformity
items.what: Independence involves making decisions free from external influence, while anti-conformity involves deliberately opposing social norms. An independent person acts based on their own values, which may sometimes align with group norms, meaning no anti-conformity is required or desired.
items.why: Conflating independence with anti-conformity leads to the incorrect assumption that an independent person must always behave unusually. A person can be fully independent and still choose to follow common social practices, simply because those practices reflect their genuine preferences.
items.example: An independent person who genuinely enjoys shaking hands when meeting new people will do so in a job interview because it reflects their preference, not because they fear being judged. They are conforming to a social norm, but from a place of independence, not social pressure.

items.title: I can define a deviant subgroup and explain how social support from one can empower individual decision-making
items.what: A deviant subgroup is a group that holds values and norms outside the dominant social norms of society. Having even one additional supporter who shares a dissenting view can significantly increase an individual's willingness to act on that view, by reducing the perceived unanimity of the majority and weakening groupthink.
items.why: Research extending Asch's findings shows that unanimity is a critical driver of conformity: break the unanimity and conformity drops sharply. A deviant subgroup, even a small one, provides this interruption, making individual decision-making more achievable.
items.example: In Asch's experiment, introducing a single confederate who gave the correct answer caused conformity rates to drop markedly, demonstrating that the presence of even one supporter reduces the pressure to match the majority's position.
